4.1.title: Therapeutic indications
4.1.text: Susvimo is indicated in adult patients for the treatment of neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) who have achieved stable disease after previously responding to intravitreal treatment with a vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitor medicinal product (see section 4.2).

4.2.title: Posology and method of administration
4.2.text:
Susvimo is intended for continuous release into the vitreous via the Contivue implant only. The initial fill and implant procedure and implant removal procedure must be performed in an operating room setting by an ophthalmologist experienced in vitreoretinal surgery and trained in the implant procedures. The implant refill-exchange procedure should be performed under strict aseptic conditions in an outpatient setting by an ophthalmologist trained in the implant refill-exchange procedure.

Patient selection

Treatment with Susvimo is initiated when disease stability after intravitreal anti-VEGF medicinal product is achieved as determined by the treating physician based on anatomic and/or visual parameters.

Posology

The recommended dose of Susvimo is 2 mg (0.02 mL) delivered via the Contivue implant with refill-exchange procedures administered every 24 weeks (approximately 6 months).

Susvimo must not be substituted for or with other formulations of ranibizumab.

Supplemental dosing with intravitreal ranibizumab injection Supplemental treatment with 0.5 mg (10 mg/mL) intravitreal ranibizumab injection may be administered in the affected eye with the Contivue implant in place if clinically necessary, based on significant decrease or reduction in visual acuity and/or extensive worsening of anatomical parameters, to reduce the risk of vision loss (see section 5.1).

Refer to the full product information for 0.5 mg (10 mg/mL) intravitreal ranibizumab injection.

Duration of treatment Duration of treatment with Susvimo should be determined by the physician and should be based on disease activity, as assessed by visual acuity and/or anatomical parameters. If, in the physician´s judgement, visual and anatomical parameters indicate that the patient is no longer benefiting from continued treatment, Susvimo refill-exchange procedures may be discontinued. The Contivue implant may be removed from the eye if deemed clinically necessary by the physician.

Implant removal and reimplantation Implant removal may be performed at the physician’s discretion, if the benefit of removal is considered to outweigh the risks of the procedure. The decision should follow a comprehensive discussion between the physician and patient about the ocular risks associated with undergoing an implant removal procedure. The benefits and risks of retaining, removing, or removing and replacing an implant are not well characterised. Refer to the device manufacturer’s implant removal procedure instructions for use.

Dose (refill-exchange) interruptions For dose (refill-exchange) interruptions related to adverse reactions see Table 1. Following a refill-exchange interruption, a refill-exchange procedure should only be performed after resolution of the adverse reaction.

Delayed or missed doses (refill-exchange) If a planned dose (refill-exchange) of Susvimo is missed, it should be administered as soon as possible and the subsequent refill-exchange procedure should be performed 24 weeks (approximately 6 months) thereafter.

Special populations

Elderly No dose adjustment is required in patients ≥ 65 years of age (see sections 5.1 and 5.2).

Renal impairment Dose adjustment is not required in patients with renal impairment (see section 5.2).

Hepatic impairment Dose adjustment is not required in patients with hepatic impairment (see section 5.2).

Paediatric population There is no relevant use of Susvimo in the paediatric population in the treatment of neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration (nAMD).

Method of administration

Susvimo is a single-dose vial for intravitreal use with the Contivue implant only.

In order to prevent medication errors, it is important to check the labels to ensure that the medicinal product being prepared and administered is Susvimo.

Susvimo should be inspected visually for particulate matter and discolouration prior to administration (see section 6.6).

Do not administer Susvimo by any route other than via the Contivue implant (e.g. not as a bolus intravitreal injection).

The initial fill and implant, and refill-exchange procedures should be performed with adequate anaesthesia under aseptic conditions to minimise the risk of intraocular infection as per standard of care.

Initial fill and implant procedure During the initial fill and implant procedure, a 1 mL Luer Lock Tip syringe is used to withdraw all of the medicinal product from the vial through a transfer needle (not included). Air is then expelled from the syringe, and the transfer needle is removed. The initial fill needle (blue cap) is then attached to the syringe and used to fill the implant with 0.02 mL of Susvimo (ranibizumab) solution for injection immediately prior to implant insertion. Once the implant is filled, it is inserted into the eye through the pars plana.

Implant refill-exchange procedure The Contivue implant is refilled with 0.02 mL of replacement Susvimo (ranibizumab) solution for injection via administration through the implant septum, which is covered by the conjunctiva and Tenon’s capsule. A 1 mL Luer Lock Tip syringe is used to withdraw all of the medicinal product from the vial through a transfer needle (not included). Air is then expelled from the syringe, and the transfer needle is removed. The refill needle (clear cap) is attached to the syringe, and the plunger rod is pushed until all air is expelled from the syringe and the dose is adjusted to 0.1 mL. The refill needle is then inserted into the implant to exchange its contents with replacement Susvimo (ranibizumab).

Read and refer to the device manufacturer´s initial fill and implant, refill-exchange and implant removal procedure Instructions for Use prior to initially filling, implanting, refilling or removing the Contivue implant.

For instructions on preparation before administration and disposal, see section 6.6.

4.3.title: Contraindications
4.3.text:
Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

Active or suspected ocular or periocular infections.

Active intraocular inflammation.

4.4.title: Special warnings and precautions for use
4.4.text:
Traceability

In order to improve the traceability of biological medicinal products, the name and the batch number of the administered product should be clearly recorded.

Educational materials

All physicians who are expected to prescribe Susvimo must ensure they have received and are familiar with the physician guide. Physicians must explain and discuss the benefits and risks of Susvimo therapy with the patient and provide them with the patient educational materials.

Bilateral treatment

In clinical trials, the majority of patients with neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) in the fellow eye received treatment with an anti-VEGF intravitreal injection and a limited number of patients received Susvimo in the fellow eye. Due to the small number of patients with bilateral treatment with Susvimo to date, the safety and efficacy of Susvimo administered in both eyes have not been established.

Implant and implant-related procedure adverse reactions

The implant and/or implant-related procedures have been associated with vitreous haemorrhage, conjunctival bleb/bleb leak, conjunctival erosion, conjunctival retraction, endophthalmitis, retinal tear and retinal detachment, traumatic cataract, device (implant) dislocation, septum dislodgement and post-surgical intraocular inflammation. All of these adverse reactions were reported during the clinical trials (see section 4.8). Patients should be instructed to report signs or symptoms, if any, that could be associated with these events without delay. In some cases, these events can present asymptomatically. The implant and the tissue overlying the implant flange should be examined carefully following the initial fill and implant and refill-exchange procedures to permit early medical or surgical intervention as necessary.

Strict adherence to the device manufacturer’s instructions for use for the initial fill and implant procedure, refill-exchange procedure and the implant removal procedure is required to minimise procedure-related risks.

Patients should be instructed not to push on the eye, rub the eye or touch the area of the eye where the implant is located for 30 days after the implant is inserted and for 7 days following the refill.

Following an implant insertion or implant removal procedure, the patient must wear a protective eye shield, and should be instructed not to remove the eye shield until advised by their physician (see section 4.7). Patients should wear the eye shield at bedtime for at least 7 nights after surgery.

Vitreous haemorrhage Vitreous haemorrhage may result in temporary vision loss. Vitrectomy may be needed in the case of a non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage (see section 4.2).

Patients on antithrombotic medicinal products (e.g. oral anticoagulants, acetylsalicylic acid, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicinal products) may be at increased risk of vitreous haemorrhage. Antithrombotic medicinal products are recommended to be temporarily interrupted prior to the implant insertion procedure.

Strict adherence to the device manufacturer’s instructions for use (e.g. appropriate pars plana laser ablation, scleral cauterisation) is required to minimise risks of vitreous haemorrhage.

Conjunctival bleb/bleb leak A conjunctival bleb/bleb leak is an encapsulated elevation of the conjunctiva above the implant flange, which may be secondary to subconjunctival thickening or fluid. Conjunctival blebs/bleb leaks may require additional surgical and/or medical management to avoid further complications, especially if the implant septum is no longer identifiable due to the conjunctival bleb/bleb leak.

Strict adherence to the device manufacturer’s instructions for use (e.g. appropriate scleral incision length, appropriate incorporation of conjunctiva and Tenon’s capsule in peritomy closure, appropriate seating of the refill needle during refill-exchange procedure) is required to minimise risks of conjunctival blebs.

Conjunctival erosion A conjunctival erosion is a full thickness degradation or breakdown of the conjunctiva in the area of the implant flange. Conjunctival erosions could be associated with an increased risk of endophthalmitis, especially if the implant becomes exposed. Surgical intervention (e.g. conjunctival/Tenon’s capsule repair) should be performed in case of conjunctival erosion with or without exposure of the implant flange.

Strict adherence to the device manufacturer’s instructions for use (e.g. appropriate incorporation of conjunctiva and Tenon’s capsule in peritomy closure, appropriate placement of conjunctival sutures to avoid contact with the implant edge) is required to minimise risks of conjunctival erosion.

Conjunctival retraction A conjunctival retraction is a recession or opening of the limbal and/or radial peritomy. Conjunctival retractions could be associated with an increased risk of endophthalmitis, especially if the implant becomes exposed. Surgical intervention (e.g. conjunctival/Tenon’s capsule repair) should be performed in case of conjunctival retraction with or without exposure of the implant flange.

Strict adherence to the device manufacturer’s instructions for use (e.g. including appropriate suturing of the conjunctiva and Tenon’s capsule to the limbus) is required to minimise risks of conjunctival retraction.

Endophthalmitis Endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular procedures and requires prompt treatment as per standard of care to reduce the risk of vision loss and to maximise recovery. The incidence of endophthalmitis following Contivue procedures was 1.6 %, compared to 0.6 % for intravitreal injections of ranibizumab in the ARCHWAY study (see section 4.8). The Susvimo dose (refill-exchange) should be withheld until resolution of endophthalmitis (see section 4.2).

Patients should not have an active or suspected ocular or periocular infection or severe systemic infection prior to any implant procedure. Proper aseptic technique should always be used when administering Susvimo.

Strict adherence to the device manufacturer’s instructions for use (e.g. appropriate sterile controls during implant insertion or refill-exchange procedures) is required to minimise risks of endophthalmitis (see section 4.8).

Retinal tear and retinal detachment Retinal tear and retinal detachment may result in vision loss if not promptly treated with an intervention (e.g. pneumatic retinopexy, vitrectomy or laser photocoagulation). Delay the Susvimo dose (refill-exchange) until the retinal tear or detachment has been treated (see section 4.2).

Careful evaluation of the retinal periphery by scleral indentation should be performed and any suspected areas of abnormal vitreo-retinal adhesion or retinal tears should be treated before inserting the implant in the eye. After insertion, the retinal periphery should be examined as per standard of care.

Strict adherence to the device manufacturer’s instructions for use (e.g. appropriate management of vitreous prolapse after pars plana incision) is required to minimise the risks of retinal tear or retinal detachment.

Device (implant) dislocation The device (implant) may dislocate or subluxate into the vitreous cavity or extend outside the vitreous cavity into or beyond the subconjunctival space. Device dislocation requires urgent surgical intervention if it is associated with a positive Seidel test, retinal detachment, appositional choroidal detachment, conjunctival opening with vitreous leak and implant expulsion (open globe), or the dislocated device is resting on or near the macula, to prevent vision loss. Patients should be instructed to avoid high risk activities including pushing, rubbing or touching their eye where the implant is located. The implant should be monitored per standard of care.

Strict adherence to the device manufacturer’s instructions for use (e.g. appropriate scleral incision length, appropriate targeting of the pars plana during laser ablation) is required to minimise risks of implant dislocation.

Septum dislodgement In clinical trials, a type of implant damage where the septum has dislodged into the body of the implant has been reported. A dilated slit lamp exam and/or dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy should be performed, to inspect the implant in the vitreous cavity through the pupil prior to and after the refill-exchange procedure to identify if septum dislodgement has occurred. Discontinue treatment with Susvimo following septum dislodgement and consider implant removal should the benefit of the removal procedure outweigh the risk (see section 4.2). The benefits and risks of retaining, removing, or removing and replacing an implant with a dislodged septum are not well characterised.

Strict adherence to the device manufacturer’s instructions for use (e.g. appropriate handling and insertion of the refill needle into the septum (avoid twisting and/or rotation)) is required to minimise the risk of septum dislodgement.

Intraocular inflammation There is a risk of intraocular inflammation following Contivue procedures (e.g. implantation, refill- exchange), consistent with the risks inherent to intraocular procedures. The majority of events experienced during clinical trials occurred during the first week following Contivue procedures and resolved within one month. Use peri-operative anti-inflammatory medicinal products per standard of care and by physician discretion. Patients should be instructed to report any signs or symptoms of intraocular inflammation to their physician.

Hypersensitivity

Patients should be instructed to report any signs or symptoms of potential ocular hypersensitivity to their physician.

Systemic effects

Systemic adverse events, including non-ocular haemorrhages and arterial thromboembolic events (ATEs), have been reported following intravitreal injection of VEGF inhibitors, or with Susvimo treatment (see section 4.8). Through week 96 of the ARCHWAY clinical trial, 12 patients (4.8 %) in the Susvimo arm and 4 patients (2.4 %) in the intravitreal arm experienced an APTC event, typically in the presence of pre-existing comorbidities.

Other

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans should be performed under specific conditions as the implant contains titanium. It is, therefore, important that patients are informed and are given an implant card which should be kept with them at all times and shown to healthcare professionals if they require an MRI scan. The device manufacturer’s instructions for use for the initial fill and implant procedure provide the scan conditions to safely perform an MRI scan for a patient with this implanted device.

Information about excipients

This medicinal product contains 0.002 mg polysorbate 20 per 0.02 mL dose. Polysorbates may cause allergic reactions. Patients need to be instructed to tell their doctor if they have any known allergies.

4.8.title: Undesirable effects
4.8.text:
Summary of the safety profile

The safety profile of Susvimo

This safety profile includes adverse reactions related to Susvimo, Contivue, the initial fill and implant, refill-exchange and implant removal procedures.

The most frequent adverse reactions overall were conjunctival haemorrhage (72.1 %), conjunctival hyperaemia (25.6 %), iritis (25 %), eye pain (20.6 %), cataract (19.1 %), conjunctival bleb/filtering bleb leak (14.9 %), vitreous floaters (13.5 %), and headache (11.6 %).

The most frequent adverse reactions during the post-operative period (within 37 days of initial implantation) were conjunctival haemorrhage (65.9 %), conjunctival hyperaemia (21.5 %), iritis (20.8 %) and eye pain (12 %).

The most frequent serious adverse reactions overall were septum dislodgement (10.1 %), conjunctival erosion (5.2 %), endophthalmitis (2.6 %), device dislocation (1.9 %), conjunctival retraction (1.9 %), conjunctival bleb/filtering bleb leak (1.7 %), cataract (1.4 %) and retinal detachment (1.2 %).

Adverse reactions that resulted in implant removal were septum dislodgement (5 %), conjunctival erosion (1.6 %), conjunctival retraction (1.2 %), endophthalmitis (1 %) and device dislocation (0.9 %).

The safety profile of intravitreal ranibizumab injections In the intravitreal injection arm of the ARCHWAY clinical trial (see section 5.1), the ocular adverse events in the study eye with the highest incidence were conjunctival haemorrhage (13.8 %), vitreous detachment (8.4 %), eye pain (7.8 %), dry eye (5.4 %), vision blurred (5.4 %) and eye irritation (5.4 %).

Non-ocular adverse events with the highest incidence in the intravitreal injection arm of the ARCHWAY clinical trial were nasopharyngitis (15 %), fall (9 %), urinary tract infection (8.4 %), arthralgia (6.6 %) and bronchitis (6 %); other non-ocular adverse events observed included allergic reactions* (rash (1.8 %), pruritus (0.6 %)) (2.4 %), anaemia (1.8 %), hypersensitivity (1.8 %), cough (1.8 %), and anxiety (1.2 %). * No events for urticaria or erythema were retrieved from the data analysed for allergic reactions.

Tabulated list of adverse reactions

The safety profile of Susvimo has been evaluated in 577 patients with nAMD in clinical trials. The median duration of treatment exposure was 244 weeks (range: 1–385 weeks). The median number of procedures, including initial fills and refill-exchanges, was 10 (range: 1–21).

Adverse reactions from clinical trials (Table 2) are listed by MedDRA System Organ Class. The corresponding frequency category for each adverse drug reaction is based on the following convention: very common (≥ 1/10), common (≥ 1/100 to < 1/10), uncommon (≥ 1/1 000 to < 1/100), rare (≥ 1/10 000 to < 1/1 000), very rare (< 1/10 000). Within each frequency grouping, adverse reactions are presented in order of decreasing seriousness.

Description of selected adverse reactions

Vitreous haemorrhage Overall, 7.5 % (43/577) of patients in the Susvimo arm experienced vitreous haemorrhage in the study eye. The majority of affected patients (31/43) experienced Grade 1 (≤ 15 letter BCVA loss from previous visit) or Grade 2 (16-30 letter BCVA loss from previous visit) events. 10 patients and 2 patients experienced a Grade 3 (>30 letters of BCVA loss from previous visit) and Grade 4 (light perception or worse) event, respectively. Of the 43 affected patients, 40 patients experienced an event that resolved, 1 patient experienced an event that resolved with sequelae, 1 patient experienced an event that was resolving, and 2 patients experienced an event that was unresolved. 34/43 patients experienced events that resolved spontaneously without medical or surgical intervention, 4 patients required a vitrectomy.

During the post-operative period, 4.5 % (26/577) of patients experienced vitreous haemorrhage. These events were attributed to the implant procedure in all 26 patients, with 7 patients having additional contributing factors. Of the affected 26 patients, 14 experienced Grade 1 events, 5 experienced Grade 2 events, 6 experienced Grade 3 events, and 1 experienced a Grade 4 event. All these events resolved.

No patients discontinued Susvimo treatment or had their implant removed due to vitreous haemorrhage.

Conjunctival bleb/Conjunctival filtering bleb leak Overall, 14.9 % (86/577) of patients in the Susvimo arm experienced conjunctival bleb/conjunctival filtering bleb leak in the study eye, with 5 % (29/577) of patients experiencing these events during the post-operative period. The majority of affected patients experienced mild (72/86) or moderate (10/86) events, and 4 patients experienced severe events. Of the 86 affected patients, 78 patients experienced an event that resolved, 1 patient experienced an event that resolved with sequelae, and 13 patients

experienced events that were unresolved. Overall, 8/86 patients experienced an event that required surgical intervention.

Conjunctival erosion Overall, 8.7 % (50/577) of patients in the Susvimo arm experienced conjunctival erosion in the study eye, with 0.3 % (2/577) of patients experiencing these events during the post-operative period. The majority of affected patients experienced mild (16/50) or moderate (23/50) events, and 11 patients experienced a severe event. Surgical intervention was required for a conjunctival erosion event in 47 patients. Of the 50 affected patients, 49 patients experienced an event that resolved, while 2 patients experienced events that were unresolved. 7/50 patients discontinued Susvimo treatment due to conjunctival erosion. Implant removal was necessary in 8/50 patients due to conjunctival erosion, with 2 patients having additional contributing factors.

Conjunctival retraction Overall, 3.5 % (20/577) of patients in the Susvimo arm experienced conjunctival retraction in the study eye, with 0.7 % (4/577) of patients experiencing these events during the postoperative period. The majority of affected patients experienced mild (9/20) or moderate (9/20) events, and 2 patients experienced a severe event. Surgical intervention was required for a conjunctival retraction event in 14 patients. Of the 20 affected patients, all patients experienced events that resolved. 6/20 patients discontinued Susvimo treatment due to conjunctival retraction. Implant removal was necessary in 6/20 patients due to conjunctival retraction, with 1 patient having additional contributing factors.

Endophthalmitis Overall, 2.8 % (16/577) of patients in the Susvimo arm experienced endophthalmitis in the study eye. Of the affected patients, 4 patients experienced moderate events, and 12 patients experienced a severe event. Of these patients, 8/16 experienced preceding or concurrent conjunctival retraction or conjunctival erosion events. Surgical intervention was required for an endophthalmitis event in 12 patients. Of the 16 affected patients, 14 patients experienced an event that resolved, 2 patients experienced an event that resolved with sequelae, and 1 patient experienced an event that was unresolved. 8/16 patients discontinued Susvimo treatment due to endophthalmitis. Implant removal was necessary in 8/16 patients due to endophthalmitis, with 1 patient having additional contributing factors.

During the comparator period of the ARCHWAY clinical trial, the incidence of endophthalmitis was 1.6 % (4/248) in the Susvimo arm compared to 0.6 % (1/167) in the intravitreal ranibizumab arm. In clinical trials the management of endophthalmitis included a flush of implant contents with 100 µL of vancomycin (1.0 mg/0.1 mL), with or without previous flush with preservative-free sodium chloride solution, in addition to standard of care.

Retinal tear and retinal detachment Overall, 0.7 % (4/577) of patients in the Susvimo arm experienced retinal tear in the study eye, with 0.2 % (1/577) of patients experiencing this event (mild) during the post-operative period. In the 4 affected patients, the events were mild (2 patients) and moderate (2 patients), and 2 patients experienced events that resolved, while 2 patients experienced events that were unresolved.

Overall, 1.6 % (9/577) of patients in the Susvimo arm experienced retinal detachment in the study eye, with 0.3 % (2/577) of patients experiencing these events during the post-operative period. All 9 patients with retinal detachment experienced severe events, which were managed with surgical intervention. Of the 9 affected patients, 7 patients experienced an event that resolved, 1 patient experienced an event that resolved with sequelae, 1 patient experienced an event that was unresolved, and 1 patient experienced an event that was resolving. Implant removal was necessary in 1/9 patients due to retinal detachment, this patient discontinued Susvimo treatment.

Device (implant) dislocation Overall, 2.4 % (14/577) of patients in the Susvimo arm experienced device dislocation in the study eye. The majority of affected patients experienced mild (3/14) or moderate (6/14) events, and 5 patients experienced severe events. Surgical intervention was required for a device location event in

13 patients, including all severe cases. Of the 14 affected patients, 13 patients experienced an event that resolved and 1 patient experienced an event that was unresolved. 8/14 patients discontinued Susvimo treatment, and implant removal was necessary in 9/14 patients, due to device dislocation.

Arterial thromboembolic events

Arterial thromboembolic events (ATEs) are adverse events potentially related to systemic VEGF inhibition. Through week 96 of the ARCHWAY clinical trial, 12 patients (4.8 %) in the Susvimo arm and 4 patients (2.4 %) in the intravitreal arm experienced an APTC event, typically in the presence of pre-existing comorbidities.

Reporting of suspected adverse reactions

Reporting suspected adverse reactions after authorisation of the medicinal product is important. It allows continued monitoring of the benefit/risk balance of the medicinal product. Healthcare professionals are asked to report any suspected adverse reactions via the national reporting system listed in Appendix V.

5.1.title: Pharmacodynamic properties
5.1.text:
Pharmacotherapeutic group: Ophthalmologicals, antineovascularisation agents, ATC code: S01LA04

Mechanism of action

Ranibizumab is a humanised recombinant monoclonal antibody fragment targeted against human vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A). It binds with high affinity to all biologically active VEGF-A isoforms (e.g. VEGF110, VEGF121 and VEGF165), thereby preventing binding of VEGF-A to its receptors VEGFR-1 and VEGFR-2.

Binding of VEGF-A to its receptors leads to endothelial cell proliferation and neovascularisation, as well as vascular leakage, which contribute to the progression of the neovascular form of age-related macular degeneration.

Immunogenicity

As with all therapeutic proteins, there is the potential for an immune response to Susvimo. Prior to treatment with Susvimo, 2.1 % (5/243) of patients with nAMD tested positive for anti-ranibizumab antibodies. After treatment with Susvimo, 13.4 % (33/247) of patients tested positive for anti- ranibizumab antibodies.

No clinically meaningful differences in the pharmacokinetics, efficacy or safety were observed in patients testing positive for anti-ranibizumab antibodies in clinical trials.

Clinical efficacy and safety

The clinical efficacy and safety of Susvimo were assessed in a randomised, visual assessor-masked, open-label active treatment-controlled study (ARCHWAY) in patients with nAMD. A total of

415 patients (248 in the Susvimo arm and 167 in the intravitreal ranibizumab arm) were enrolled and treated in this study.

Patients were diagnosed with any type of macular choroidal neovascularisation (CNV) related to nAMD within the 9 months prior to screening and received ≥ 3 doses of anti-VEGF intravitreal agents in the study eye within the last 6 months prior to screening. At the screening visit, patients received an additional intravitreal injection of 0.5 mg ranibizumab if they received only 3 doses of anti-VEGF intravitreal agents within the last 6 months and/or if the last treatment received prior to screening was not 0.5 mg ranibizumab. Each patient had a demonstrated response to anti-VEGF intravitreal agents defined as: overall decrease in nAMD disease activity detected on spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) and stable or improved vision.

Patients were randomised in a 3:2 ratio to receive continuous delivery of Susvimo via the implant every 24 weeks or intravitreal injections of 0.5 mg ranibizumab every 4 weeks. For patients randomised to the Susvimo arm, supplemental treatment with 0.5 mg intravitreal ranibizumab injections was available at weeks 16, 20, 40, 44, 64, 68, 88, and 92 if one of the following criteria was met and due to nAMD disease activity: a loss of 15 early treatment diabetic retinopathy study (ETDRS) letters from the best recorded BCVA value on study, an increase of 150 microns from the lowest central subfield thickness (CST) value on study, or a loss of 10 letters from the highest BCVA value associated with an increase of 100 microns from the lowest CST value.

The baseline demographics were generally balanced across treatment groups; 43/415 (10.4%) patients were younger than 65 years of age and the mean [SD] age was 75 [7.91] years. The majority of patients were female (59 %). The mean [SD] BCVA score at baseline was 74.8 [10.4] letters.

Prior to study treatment, a median of 4 doses of anti-VEGF intravitreal agents were administered in the study eye of the patients in the Susvimo and intravitreal ranibizumab arms. The mean [SD] change in visual acuity in the study eye from diagnosis of nAMD to baseline was 11.3 [13.8] letters. Of the patients assessed for supplemental treatment in the Susvimo arm, 98.4 %, 94.6 %, 94.8 % and 94.7 % did not receive supplemental treatment in the first, second, third and fourth treatment intervals, respectively. Across all four treatment intervals, 31/246 patients (12.6%) received supplemental treatment, and 215/246 patients (87.4%) did not receive supplemental treatment. Of the 31 patients, 18 patients (58.1%) received only one supplemental treatment.

The primary efficacy endpoint of change from baseline in BCVA score averaged over week 36 and week 40 demonstrated Susvimo to be equivalent to intravitreal ranibizumab injections administered every 4 weeks. Detailed efficacy results are shown in Table 3 and Figure 1.

Consistent results were observed across patient subgroup analyses for mean change from baseline in BCVA score averaged over weeks 36 and 40 (age, gender, number of prior anti-VEGF intravitreal injections and baseline BCVA score) and centre point thickness (CPT) at week 36 (age and gender).

Leakage of blood and fluid from CNV may cause retinal thickening or oedema and/or intraretinal/subretinal haemorrhage, resulting in vision loss. The anatomical parameter CPT [measured from internal limiting membrane (ILM) to retinal pigment epithelium] was assessed. At week 36, a similar adjusted mean change in CPT was observed between the Susvimo arm and intravitreal ranibizumab arm patients (5.4 microns vs 2.6 microns, respectively). This corresponded to a difference in adjusted means of 2.8 microns (95 % CI: -6.2, 11.8) between arms.

Paediatric population

The European Medicines Agency has waived the obligation to submit the results of studies with Susvimo in all subsets of the paediatric population for nAMD (see section 4.2 for information on paediatric use).

5.2.title: Pharmacokinetic properties
5.2.text:
Absorption

Susvimo delivered via the Contivue implant provides continuous delivery of ranibizumab into the vitreous, with the release of ranibizumab decreasing over time as the concentration in the implant decreases. The observed serum and observed aqueous humour ranibizumab concentrations with Susvimo are maintained below the maximum and above the minimum concentrations achieved with monthly 0.5 mg intravitreal ranibizumab.

In the ARCHWAY clinical trial, the mean (± SD) maximum ranibizumab serum concentration (Cmax) was 0.48 (± 0.17) ng/mL and median (range) time to maximum serum concentration (Tmax) was 26 (1 – 89) days following implant insertion. Following the initial fill and refill-exchange procedures with Susvimo in patients with nAMD, maximum serum concentrations of ranibizumab were below the ranibizumab concentration necessary to inhibit the biological activity of VEGF by 50 %.

Distribution

Ranibizumab is distributed from the vitreous to the aqueous humour and serum. Based on population pharmacokinetics analysis, the ranibizumab concentrations in aqueous humour decrease with a half-life of approximately 15 weeks and the ranibizumab serum concentrations decrease with a half-life of approximately 29 weeks. Ranibizumab did not accumulate in serum when administered with refill-exchange procedures every 24 weeks.

Biotransformation and elimination

The metabolism of Susvimo has not been directly studied. Susvimo is a monoclonal antibody fragment. Antibodies are cleared principally by catabolism.

Special populations

Elderly In the population pharmacokinetic analysis of nAMD patients with Susvimo, the age of patients ranged from 50 to 92 years old. Age did not have a significant effect on the pharmacokinetics of Susvimo.

Renal impairment No formal studies have been conducted to examine the pharmacokinetics of Susvimo in patients with renal impairment. In a population pharmacokinetic analysis of nAMD patients with Susvimo, 73 % (266 of 364) had renal impairment (44 % mild [CrCL 60 to < 90 mL/min], 27 % moderate [CrCL 30 to < 60 mL/min] and 2 % severe [CrCL < 30 mL/min]). This analysis showed that systemic clearance of ranibizumab was slightly lower in renally impaired patients but was not clinically significant.

Hepatic impairment No formal studies have been conducted to examine the pharmacokinetics of Susvimo in patients with hepatic impairment. However, systemic exposure of Susvimo is low, with concentrations remaining below the ranibizumab concentration necessary to inhibit the biological activity of VEGF by 50 % (11-27 ng/mL). Therefore, no dose adjustment is considered necessary in this population (see section 4.2).
